title: Short Stuff: Dead Bodies and Airline Codes
summary: Short Stuff episode on the "Jim Wilson" airline code, which reportedly means a dead body (human remains) on an American Airlines flight. The hosts review the evidence: a HowStuffWorks article, a National Funeral Director's Association page, a Wall Street Journal mention, and a search redirect to American Airlines' human remains site. American Airlines reportedly denied the code. They then cover practical issues of transporting a body (funeral directors on each end, costs from about $2,000 to $15,000 or more for international shipment, driving a body across states, travel insurance, cremated remains as carry-on through TSA, and a New York Giants lineman's TSA luggage incident). The episode closes with other airline secret codes: Code Rabo (hijacking-related), 7700 (general emergency), 7600 (radio failure), and Code Adam (missing child).

segments.title: Opening and the Jim Wilson airline code
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic: the Jim Wilson airline code, supposedly American Airlines' code for a dead body on a plane. They note American Airlines reportedly denied it.

segments.title: Evidence for the Jim Wilson code
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why a code would be unnecessary since bodies ride in the cargo hold, the National Funeral Directors Association page, a Wall Street Journal article, the Jim Wilson website, and a search that redirects to American Airlines' human remains site. Other airlines reportedly use HR or HUM.

segments.title: Costs and logistics of shipping a body
segments.summary: Shipping a body requires a funeral director at each end because airlines accept only known shippers. Costs range from about $2,000 to $15,000, higher internationally, and train is cheaper than plane. Driving remains yourself is possible but state embalming laws complicate it. Travel insurance can cover repatriation.

segments.title: International costs and air trays
segments.summary: International shipment can cost up to about $25,000 and requires translated documents. Caskets must sit in special trays in the cargo hold, and one early tray maker was reportedly the Jim Wilson Company.

segments.title: Cremated remains and TSA
segments.summary: Cremated remains are cheaper and easier to ship and can usually be carried on, though TSA screening and urn materials matter. A New York Giants lineman, J. Francis, reportedly complained on Twitter after TSA opened his checked bag and his mother's remains were spilled.

segments.title: Airline secret codes
segments.summary: The hosts list airline emergency codes: Code Rabo (hijacking), 7500 (hijack), 7600 (radio failure), 7700 (general emergency), and Code Adam (missing child).

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up the Jim Wilson topic and close the show.
